column1: #tags column:3
Name the five regions of a CMOS inverter's transfer curve.
column2: A: NMOS off, output at \(V_{DD}\). B: NMOS saturated, PMOS linear. C: both saturated around \(V_M\) (the steep segment). D: NMOS linear, PMOS saturated. E: PMOS off, output at 0. Static current flows only for \(V_{TN} < V_{in} < V_{DD} - |V_{TP}|\).

column1: Give the switching threshold of a square-law CMOS inverter.
column2: \(V_M = (V_{TN}\sqrt r + V_{DD} - |V_{TP}|)/(1 + \sqrt r)\) with \(r = k_n/k_p\); it equals \(V_{DD}/2\) for a symmetric inverter and moves only with \(\sqrt r\), so large sizing changes shift it modestly.

column1: How are noise margins defined, and what are they for a symmetric square-law inverter?
column2: \(NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}\), \(NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}\), with \(V_{IL}\), \(V_{IH}\) the unity-gain points. Symmetric, λ = 0: both equal \((3V_{DD} + 2V_{TH})/8\), about 40–45% of the supply.

column1: What sets an inverter's gain at its switching threshold?
column2: \(|A_v| = (g_{mn} + g_{mp})/(g_{dsn} + g_{dsp}) \approx 2/(\lambda V_{ov})\) for a symmetric square-law inverter: tens to hundreds, so the output swings over roughly 5–20 mV of input. Gain above 1 is what lets a chain of gates regenerate logic levels.

column1: Why should PMOS sizing use the drive-current ratio rather than the mobility ratio in modern processes?
column2: Electrons velocity-saturate more than holes, so velocity saturation cuts the NMOS current more than the PMOS current. The saturated drive ratio is therefore below \(\mu_n/\mu_p\), and a narrower PMOS balances the inverter.

column1: What is the lowest supply at which a CMOS inverter still has gain?
column2: \(V_{DD,min} = 2V_T\ln(1 + n)\), about 36–50 mV at room temperature, from subthreshold operation; practical logic needs a few hundred millivolts for speed and margin.

column1: What makes up an inverter's load capacitance?
column2: \(C_L = C_{int} + C_{ext}\): its own drain capacitances plus doubled gate-drain (Miller) capacitance, and the gate capacitance of the fan-out plus the wire.

column1: How is the RC model of a switching transistor built?
column2: \(t_p = \ln 2\,R_{eq}C_L\) with \(R_{eq}\) the average of \(V/I\) over the output transition, approximately \(3V_{DD}/(4I_{sat})\); \(R_{eq}\) scales as 1/W.

column1: Why can't upsizing an inverter make it arbitrarily fast?
column2: Its own diffusion capacitance grows with size: \(t_p = t_{p0}(1 + C_{ext}/(SC_{int,ref}))\) approaches the size-independent intrinsic delay \(t_{p0} = 0.69R_{ref}C_{int,ref}\), and a bigger gate loads its own driver.

column1: What is the FO4 delay and why is it used?
column2: The delay of an inverter driving four copies of itself, \(t_{p0}(1 + 4/\gamma)\); it normalizes speed across processes, so designs are compared in FO4 per cycle. With \(\gamma\) = 1 (the course's \(p_{inv} = 1\)) it is \(5t_{p0}\); with \(\gamma \approx 0.5\) it is \(9t_{p0}\).

column1: Why does a ring oscillator's stage delay exceed the step-input delay?
column2: Each stage is driven by the previous stage's slow ramp, not a step, so the driver turns on gradually and both devices conduct for part of the transition; the 19-02 lab measured almost twice the step value.

column1: How do delay and energy scale with supply voltage?
column2: Energy per transition \(\propto V_{DD}^2\); delay \(\propto V_{DD}/(V_{DD} - V_{TH})^\alpha\) rises sharply near threshold. The energy-delay product is minimized near \(3V_{TH}/(3 - \alpha)\).

column1: How are NAND and NOR gates sized for unit drive?
column2: NAND-N: series NMOS of width N, parallel PMOS of width μ. NOR-N: series PMOS of width Nμ, parallel NMOS of width 1. Input capacitance \((N + \mu)/(1 + \mu)\) and \((1 + N\mu)/(1 + \mu)\) of an inverter's.

column1: What is the Elmore constant, and how does it give a delay estimate? Why does stack delay grow quadratically with fan-in?
column2: \(\tau_E = \sum_m C_mR_{km}\), each capacitance times the resistance it shares with the output path; the 50% delay estimate is \(0.69\tau_E\) (and \(\tau_E\) itself bounds the delay from above for RC trees). Internal stack nodes each discharge through part of the stack, adding \(RcN(N-1)/2\).

column1: What does pseudo-NMOS trade away?
column2: It replaces the PMOS network with one always-on PMOS: fewer transistors (N + 1) but a nonzero \(V_{OL}\) set by the k ratio, and static power \(V_{DD}I_{load}\) whenever the output is low.

column1: Why does an NMOS pass transistor pass a weak 1?
column2: It stops conducting when its source reaches \(V_{DD} - V_{TN}\), and the body effect raises \(V_{TN}\) as the source rises; transmission gates pair NMOS and PMOS to pass both levels.

column1: What is charge sharing in a dynamic gate?
column2: After precharge, opening a path to an uncharged internal node splits the output's charge, lowering it to \(V_{DD}C_L/(C_L + C_a)\), or by \((C_a/C_L)(V_{DD} - V_{TN})\) if the connecting device cuts off first.

column1: Why do domino gates add a static inverter after each dynamic stage?
column2: Dynamic outputs only fall during evaluation, so feeding them directly to another dynamic gate could discharge it erroneously; the inverter makes every input rise monotonically. The cost: only non-inverting logic.

column1: Write the logical-effort delay model.
column2: \(d = gh + p\) in units of \(\tau = 0.69RC_{inv}\): logical effort g (INV 1, NAND2 4/3, NOR2 5/3), electrical effort \(h = C_{out}/C_{in}\), parasitic delay p.

column1: What are the path efforts G, B, H, F?
column2: \(G = \prod g_i\), branching \(B = \prod b_i\) with \(b = (C_{on} + C_{off})/C_{on}\), \(H = C_{out}/C_{in}\) of the path, and \(F = GBH\).

column1: What is the minimum delay of an N-stage path?
column2: \(\hat D = NF^{1/N} + P\), reached when every stage bears the same effort \(F^{1/N}\); size backward from the load with \(C_{in} = gC_{out}/\hat f\).

column1: What is the best stage effort and number of stages?
column2: ρ solves \(\rho(\ln\rho - 1) = p_{inv}\): 3.59 for \(p_{inv} = 1\), so about 4. Use \(N \approx \log_4 F\) stages; delay is within about 9% of optimal for stage efforts 2.4–6.

column1: Why is an FO4 delay 5τ in logical-effort units?
column2: An inverter has g = 1 and \(p_{inv} = 1\); driving four copies gives h = 4, so d = 4 + 1 = 5. The course takes \(p_{inv} = \gamma = 1\); with \(\gamma \approx 0.5\) the FO4 is 4.5τ.

column1: What is a wire's resistance from its geometry?
column2: \(R = \rho L/(Wt) = R_\square\,L/W\) with sheet resistance \(R_\square = \rho/t\); in narrow copper, surface and grain-boundary scattering raise resistivity well above bulk.

column1: What is the 50% delay of a distributed RC line?
column2: 0.38 RC for a step at one end and an open far end: the lumped model's 0.69 RC overestimates by about 80%, and the Elmore constant is RC/2.

column1: Why do repeaters make long-wire delay linear in length?
column2: An unbuffered wire's delay grows as \(L^2\) (both R and C grow with L). Cutting it into k segments with repeaters makes each segment's \(RC\) fall as \(1/k^2\); at the optimum the total is about \(2.4\sqrt{R_0C_0rc}\,L\) (2.40 with 0.69 and 0.38, 2.41 with ln 2 and 0.379).

column1: What is the Miller coupling factor?
column2: Coupling capacitance counts 0 times if the neighbor switches the same way, once if it is quiet, twice if it switches opposite; it makes a wire's effective load and delay depend on its neighbors.

column1: How do wires scale with technology?
column2: Resistance per length rises as \(1/S^2\) while capacitance per length stays about 0.2 fF/µm, so local wires keep their RC but global wires slow down relative to gates; repeated delay per length grows about 1.2× per node.

column1: Why does charging a capacitor dissipate half the energy no matter the resistance?
column2: The supply delivers \(CV_{DD}^2\); the capacitor stores \(\tfrac12CV_{DD}^2\), and the rest is lost in the charging resistance independent of its value; discharging dissipates the stored half.

column1: Give the dynamic power formula and what α means.
column2: \(P = \alpha CV_{DD}^2f\), with α the 0→1 transitions per node per cycle (1 for clocks, far less for most logic).

column1: How does subthreshold leakage depend on threshold voltage?
column2: Exponentially: slope \(S = nV_T\ln 10\) ≈ 60n mV/decade at 300 K, so each S of threshold reduction multiplies leakage by 10; leakage also rises steeply with temperature.

column1: What is the stack effect?
column2: Two off transistors in series leak far less than one (often ~10× or more), mainly because the intermediate node rises, reducing DIBL and giving the top device a negative \(V_{GS}\).

column1: Name four low-power techniques and their costs.
column2: Clock gating (control logic, timing of the enable); power gating (wake time and energy, sleep transistors); DVFS (regulators, latency); multi-\(V_{TH}\) cells (leakage vs speed per path). Parallelism at lower voltage trades area for energy.

column1: Why is there a minimum-energy supply voltage?
column2: Lowering V cuts switching energy as \(V^2\) but slows gates exponentially in subthreshold, so leakage energy per operation rises; the optimum solves \(L_de^{-x}(x-2) = 2\alpha\), typically 0.2–0.4 V.

column1: State the setup and hold constraints with skew and jitter.
column2: Setup: \(T_c \ge t_{pcq} + t_{pd} + t_{setup} - \delta + t_{jitter}\). Hold: \(t_{ccq} + t_{cd} \ge t_{hold} + \delta\), with δ = capture − launch clock arrival. Late capture helps setup and hurts hold.

column1: Why can't a hold violation be fixed by slowing the clock?
column2: The hold check compares the same clock edge at launch and capture; the period does not appear, so only added data-path delay (or less skew) fixes it.

column1: What limits the benefit of deeper pipelining?
column2: \(T_c = t_L/N + t_o\): the fixed sequencing overhead \(t_o\) per stage becomes a growing share, latency grows as \(t_L + Nt_o\), and hazards and power add costs; one well-known study put the optimum at 6–8 FO4 of logic per stage.

column1: What is time borrowing?
column2: With two-phase latches, a slow half-cycle of logic can run into the next half-cycle while the latch is transparent, up to \(T_c/2 - t_{setup}\), so the cycle constraint applies to loop totals instead of each stage.

column1: How does a metastable latch resolve, and what is MTBF?
column2: The voltage difference grows as \(e^{t/\tau}\) with \(\tau = C/g_m\); \(\text{MTBF} = e^{t_r/\tau}/(T_0f_{clk}f_{data})\), and each extra synchronizer stage multiplies it by \(e^{T_c/\tau}\).

column1: Why must a multi-bit bus not be synchronized bit by bit?
column2: Each bit may resolve on a different cycle, so the receiver can see a mix of old and new values; use a handshake, Gray-coded pointers or an asynchronous FIFO.

column1: What two ratios govern a 6T SRAM cell?
column2: Cell ratio \(k_N/k_A\) (about 1.5–2.5) keeps the read disturbance below the inverter threshold. Pull-up ratio \(k_P/k_A\) must be small enough for the written node to fall below \(V_{TN}\): about 0.67 or less for 19-08's cell (textbook W/L rules near 1–1.5 absorb the PMOS's lower mobility). Together: \(k_P < k_A < k_N\).

column1: What is static noise margin, and why is read SNM smaller than hold SNM?
column2: The side of the largest square that fits inside the butterfly curves' smaller lobe. During a read the access transistor pulls the low node up, degrading one inverter's curve and shrinking the lobe.

column1: Why does SRAM sense small bitline swings?
column2: The cell current is tiny and the bitline long, so a full swing takes far too long. The bitline develops a small swing \(\Delta V\) (about 100 mV, set by the amplifier's offset) in \(C_{BL}\Delta V/I_{cell}\), and the sense amplifier regenerates it to full rail in \(\tau\ln(V_{DD}/\Delta V)\).

column1: How do SRAM arrays reach high yield with billions of cells?
column2: Each cell's failure probability is \(Q(\mu/\sigma)\); array yield is \(e^{-NQ}\), so cells are designed for about 6σ margin, plus row/column redundancy and ECC to repair the few failures.

column1: Why does SRAM usually set a chip's minimum operating voltage?
column2: Its minimum-size transistors have the largest random threshold variation, and read and write margins collapse at low voltage; separate SRAM rails, assist circuits and 8T cells extend it.

column1: What are contacted and uncontacted gate pitch?
column2: The spacing of adjacent gates with a contact between them (gate + two contact-to-gate spaces + contact, 8λ in the chapter's rules) versus without (gate + poly spacing, 5λ); internal stack nodes are left uncontacted.

column1: How does an Euler path give a gate an unbroken diffusion strip?
column2: If one ordering of the inputs is an Euler path of both the pull-down and the pull-up graphs, the transistors can be placed in that order in both strips with shared diffusion and no breaks.

column1: What is a standard cell?
column2: A pre-laid-out gate of fixed height (a whole number of routing tracks) and variable width, with power rails at top and bottom, so cells abut in rows; SKY130's hd site is 0.46 × 2.72 µm, 9 met1 tracks. A block's core area is the total cell area divided by the utilization (about 0.6–0.8); routed gate-density figures already include utilization.

column1: What do DRC, LVS and antenna checks protect against?
column2: DRC: geometry the fab cannot build reliably. LVS: a layout that does not match the schematic. Antenna: long metal connected to a small gate charging during plasma etch and damaging its oxide, fixed with jumpers or diodes.

column1: What does logic synthesis do, in three steps?
column2: It translates RTL into a generic Boolean network, optimizes that network technology-independently, then maps it onto the cells of a standard-cell library (technology mapping), sizing cells and buffering nets to meet timing, area and power constraints.

column1: How does tree-covering technology mapping find an optimal cover?
column2: It splits the subject network into trees, then by dynamic programming over each tree's nodes (inputs first) picks, for every node, the library pattern matching there that minimizes cost (area, or arrival time) plus the best costs already found for the pattern's inputs.

column1: What is an NLDM table in a Liberty file?
column2: A non-linear delay model: a 2-D table of a cell arc's delay (and output slew) against input slew and output load capacitance; tools interpolate bilinearly between the table points.

column1: Define arrival time, required time and slack on a timing graph.
column2: Arrival time: the latest time a signal settles at a node (max over fan-in of input arrival plus arc delay). Required time: the latest it may settle and still meet the capture check (min over fan-out). Slack = required − arrival; negative slack is a violation.

column1: Write the setup and hold slacks between two flip-flops (19-10 notation).
column2: Setup: \(\text{slack} = T_c + L_2 - t_{setup} - U - (L_1 + t_{pcq} + t_{pd})\). Hold: \(\text{slack} = (L_1 + t_{ccq} + t_{cd}) - (L_2 + t_{hold} + U)\). Negative means failing in both; the period does not appear in the hold check.

column1: What is CRPR (clock reconvergence pessimism removal)?
column2: With on-chip-variation derates, the shared part of the launch and capture clock paths is derated late for one and early for the other, which is impossible on one physical wire; CRPR adds back that common-path difference to the slack.

column1: Why do statistical (POCV) margins grow only as \(\sqrt N\) along a path?
column2: Independent random gate delay variations add in quadrature: N stages of standard deviation σ give \(\sigma\sqrt N\), so the relative margin shrinks as paths get deeper, unlike a flat percentage derate.

column1: What are false paths and multicycle paths?
column2: False paths are structural paths that can never be sensitized functionally (excluded from timing); multicycle paths are allowed more than one clock period by design (their setup check moves by N periods, and the hold check must be moved back to match).

column1: How is a core area sized from cell area?
column2: Core area = total standard-cell area ÷ target utilization (typically 0.5–0.8), leaving room for buffering, routing and timing repair.

column1: What is the worst IR drop on a strap carrying uniformly distributed current \(I\) with total resistance \(R\)?
column2: Fed from one end: \(IR/2\) at the far end. Fed from both ends: \(IR/8\) at the middle. Feeding both ends cuts the drop fourfold.

column1: What is the half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) of a net?
column2: The half-perimeter of the smallest box enclosing its pins, \((x_{max} - x_{min}) + (y_{max} - y_{min})\): exact for 2- and 3-pin nets' Steiner length and a lower bound otherwise; placers minimize its sum.

column1: How does quadratic placement work?
column2: Treat each net as springs and minimize total squared wirelength; setting the gradient to zero gives a sparse linear system (a graph Laplacian with fixed pads) solved for x and y, followed by spreading to remove overlaps.

column1: Give the zero-skew tapping point between two clock subtrees.
column2: At distance \(x = [t_2 - t_1 + rL(C_2 + cL/2)]/[r(C_1 + C_2 + cL)]\) from subtree 1 along a wire of length \(L\), resistance \(r\) and capacitance \(c\) per length, from equating the Elmore delays; if \(x\) falls outside \([0, L]\), the wire must be lengthened (snaked).

column1: What does Lee's maze router guarantee?
column2: Breadth-first wave expansion over the routing grid from source to target finds a shortest path around obstacles if one exists, at the cost of memory and time proportional to the grid area.

column1: How much shorter can a rectilinear Steiner tree be than a spanning tree?
column2: At most by a third: Hwang's bound says the rectilinear minimum spanning tree is at most 3/2 times the minimum Steiner tree, whose extra points can be restricted to the Hanan grid.

column1: Name four signoff checks before tape-out.
column2: Static timing at all corners and modes with extracted parasitics; DRC; LVS; antenna, electromigration and IR-drop (power integrity) checks; plus logic equivalence and DFT checks.

column1: State the Williams–Brown defect level.
column2: \(\text{DL} = 1 - Y^{1-T}\) for yield \(Y\) and fault coverage \(T\); near full coverage \(\text{DL} \approx (1-T)(-\ln Y)\), so each extra nine of coverage cuts escapes about tenfold.

column1: What is a stuck-at fault, and where are the fault sites?
column2: A line permanently at 0 or 1. Every stem and every fanout branch is a site with two faults, so a circuit with \(n\) lines has \(2n\) single stuck-at faults before collapsing.

column1: What three things must a test do to detect a stuck-at fault?
column2: Activate it (drive the line to the opposite of the stuck value), propagate the difference to an output (non-controlling values on side inputs), and justify the required values back to primary inputs.

column1: How many random patterns detect a fault of per-pattern detection probability \(p\) with confidence \(P_d\)?
column2: \(N = \ln(1 - P_d)/\ln(1 - p) \approx -\ln(1-P_d)/p\); a fault needing \(k\) specific inputs has \(p = 2^{-k}\), which is why wide ANDs resist random patterns.

column1: How many clock cycles does a scan test of \(P\) patterns on chains of length \(L\) take?
column2: \(P(L + 1) + L\): each pattern shifts \(L\) bits and captures once, unloading overlaps the next load, and a final unload adds \(L\).

column1: Why does test compression work?
column2: Each pattern needs specified values only in a few care bits; a linear decompressor expands a few tester channels into many internal chains satisfying those bits, and a compactor shrinks the responses.

column1: What is MISR aliasing, and how likely is it?
column2: A faulty response stream compacting to the good signature; for an \(n\)-bit MISR the fraction of error streams that alias is about \(2^{-n}\) (exactly \((2^{n(m-1)} - 1)/(2^{nm} - 1)\) for \(m\) words). A single-bit error never aliases.

column1: How long is March C−, and what does it detect?
column2: \(10n\) operations for \(n\) cells; it detects stuck-at, transition, address-decoder and idempotent coupling faults.

column1: Verification versus validation versus test?
column2: Verification: does the design implement its specification (pre-silicon). Validation: is the specification right, and does the real chip work in the system. Test: is this die free of manufacturing defects.

column1: Code coverage versus functional coverage?
column2: Code coverage is measured automatically from the RTL (lines, branches, conditions, toggles, FSM states). Functional coverage is written from the verification plan (coverpoints, bins, crosses). Neither shows that results were checked.

column1: Expected random samples to fill \(n\) equally likely coverage bins? And with unequal bins?
column2: \(nH_n \approx n\ln n + 0.577n + \tfrac12\). Unequal: \(E[T] = \sum_{S \ne \emptyset} (-1)^{|S|+1}/p(S) \ge 1/p_{min}\); the rarest bin dominates.

column1: What do |-> and |=> mean in SVA, and what is a vacuous pass?
column2: \(a\ |\text{->}\ b\) checks \(b\) in the cycle \(a\) matches; \(a\ |\text{=>}\ b\) checks it one cycle later. An implication whose antecedent never matches passes vacuously, having checked nothing.

column1: Why does a round-robin arbiter bound waiting at \(N - 1\) grants?
column2: Each grant to another requester moves the search pointer strictly closer to a pending requester (its cyclic distance drops by at least 1), so at most \(N - 1\) others can be served first. Fixed priority has no bound.

column1: Why are ROBDDs useful for equivalence checking, and what is their weakness?
column2: For a fixed variable order each Boolean function has exactly one ROBDD, so two circuits are equivalent iff their (miter) diagrams match; but size depends on the order (\(\sum x_iy_i\): \(2n\) interleaved, \(2^{n+1}-2\) separated) and multipliers are exponential in every order.

column1: What does bounded model checking prove?
column2: Only that no property violation exists within \(k\) cycles of reset; it becomes a proof when \(k\) reaches the diameter of the reachable state graph, or when combined with an induction step.

column1: What is a counterexample to induction (CTI)?
column2: An unreachable state that satisfies the property but steps to a violation; it shows the property is not inductive, not that the design is wrong. Fix by increasing \(k\) or adding a strengthening lemma.

column1: Emulation versus FPGA prototyping?
column2: Emulators run the RTL on purpose-built hardware with deep debug visibility, fast compiles and huge capacity; FPGA prototypes run faster (vendors claim up to tens of MHz) for software work but with little visibility and longer bring-up.
